How to read a target

To “read” a target means to understand, before you shoot, how it flies: where it appears, how fast it moves, where it turns, climbs or drops. Experienced shooters do this at each stand, and it often makes the difference between a hit and a miss. It matters in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting alike.

Start with the target menu: which traps, in what order, and whether there are special targets. Then watch closely while the targets are shown (the presentation). In Sporting™ the targets of a stand are shown before shooting to the first shooter of the squad. Doubles on report are not shown. Compak® Sporting has its own way of showing targets. The details are in Viewing the targets.

Ask yourself simple questions. Where do I first see the target clearly? That is your pick-up point, where your eyes start following it. Where is it easiest to break? That is your break point. There the target should still be clearly visible, not dropping behind trees or flying beyond a shooting limit.

Tip: How the hold point, the pick-up point and the break point work together is explained in Three points: pick-up, hold and break.

Note the speed, distance and angle, and what the target is doing: climbing, slowing down or falling. Wind can lift a target or push it down, and a dark tree line or a bright sky changes how you see it. A target that is slowing down needs less lead than one at full speed.

Watch how others shoot, but think for yourself: each shooter has their own tempo. While the targets are being shown, many coaches suggest following them with your eyes only.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Not allowed anywhere on the ground. The first time, the referee gives a warning. If you do it again, your next hit target is scored as a miss (zero).

Compak® Sporting

Not allowed outside the shooting stations, or while another squad member is shooting. While the targets are being shown, the gun is open and unloaded.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Sporting™ trajectories are graded by difficulty class: class A is broken by an average shooter more than 80% of the time, class B 60–80%, class C 40–60%. Do not be upset if you miss a class C target: it is meant to be hard. Reading targets is easier to learn with a qualified coach who shows you what to look at.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 2 · Difficulty classes A, B and C

Key points

  • Menu first, then watch closely while the targets are shown.
  • Find where you first see the target clearly and where you will break it.
  • Note speed, angle, wind, background and whether the target is slowing.
  • Follow with your eyes; in Sporting™ mock shooting is not allowed anywhere on the ground, in Compak® Sporting off the stations and while someone else shoots.
  • Sporting™ difficulty classes: class A is broken by an average shooter more than 80% of the time, class B 60–80%, class C 40–60%.

Did you know?

In Sporting™ doubles on report are not shown, but you have already seen both targets: doubles are made only of targets shown as singles from the same stand.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. What is the break point?

    1. Where you plan to break the target
    2. Where the trap that throws it stands
    3. Where the target lands on the ground
    Answer

    Where you plan to break the target

    The break point is the place on the trajectory that you choose in advance.

  2. In Sporting™, while the targets are being shown, may you mount the gun and swing it along the target's line?

    1. Yes, it is good preparation
    2. No, that is mock shooting
    3. Yes, if the gun is unloaded
    Answer

    No, that is mock shooting

    Follow with your eyes only. Nobody may fire or pretend to fire while the targets are being shown, and guns stay open and unloaded until the referee allows them to be closed.

    Chapter 16 · Presentation of targets

  3. What share of class C targets does an average shooter break in Sporting™?

    1. More than 80%
    2. 60 to 80%
    3. 40 to 60%
    Answer

    40 to 60%

    Class C is the hardest: 40–60%. Class A is over 80%, class B 60–80%.
